The paper asks how to support that reshuffling inside processing-in-memory hardware without building a separate expensive circuit for it.
743.wh: The hard part is that the computation is trying to save cost in two places at once. First, quantized networks save cost by representing values with very few levels and replacing heavy multiplication with bit-wise accumulation. Second, processing-in-memory saves cost by doing work near memory, because moving values back and forth can consume more time and energy than the arithmetic itself. But BitNetv2 adds a new operation before the cheap layer: the Hadamard Transform. That transform helps accuracy because it spreads concentrated input values more evenly across quantization levels, yet it also introduces extra additions, wiring, and data movement. A hardware design that simply bolts this transform onto an existing bit-wise accelerator may give back much of the efficiency it was meant to save. The central tension is therefore structural: the model needs the transform to protect accuracy, but the hardware cannot afford to treat it as an unrelated second pipeline.
743.naive: A smart beginner would build two blocks. One block would perform the Hadamard Transform to flatten the inputs before quantization. Another block would perform the BitLinear accumulation used by the matmul-free layer. This is simple to reason about, because each mathematical operation receives its own circuit and its own data path. It fails because the expensive part in this setting is not just adding numbers. It is also moving small values through wires, reading them from memory, and reducing many partial results into one output. Separate blocks duplicate adder trees and force data to travel between stages. In a processing-in-memory design, that duplication directly attacks the reason for using the architecture in the first place.
743.ap: The paper's central move is to notice that the two operations are not as different as they look. The Hadamard Transform can be read as a repeated pattern of adding and subtracting pairs of values, then combining those results again in a recursive butterfly shape. BitLinear accumulation also gathers many low-precision contributions through an addition tree. The authors observe that the Hadamard recursion can be represented as linear combinations whose weights come from a tiny set, W in {-1, 0, 1}. That makes it close in spirit to the bit-wise accumulation already needed for the neural layer. Instead of paying for two separate reduction paths, the proposed accelerator builds a butterfly-shaped adder-tree circuit for the transform and reuses part of that same circuit as the accumulation tree for BitLinear. The idea is hardware reuse based on a shared mathematical skeleton.
743.mech: The input is a block of low-precision neural values that will pass through a BitNetv2-style layer. Before those values are quantized and accumulated, the system applies a Hadamard Transform so that the input distribution is flattened rather than concentrated around the center. Mechanically, the transform breaks the input vector into pairs, forms simple sums and differences, then repeats that combining pattern across larger and larger groups. This forms the butterfly pattern: values meet in pairs, split into new combined values, and meet again at the next level. The paper interprets this recursion as a sequence of linear combinations using only -1, 0, and 1 as weights, which means the operation can be done with sign changes, skips, and additions rather than full multipliers. The same accelerator must also run BitLinear, where bit-wise contributions are accumulated into output values. The proposed processing-in-memory design therefore places a butterfly-shaped adder tree near memory. During the Hadamard stage, the tree carries out the recursive pairwise combinations. During the BitLinear stage, reused portions of the tree collect bit-wise partial sums. What comes out is the same functional sequence the model needs, but with a unified reduction datapath rather than separate hardware and extra data transfers.
743.math: The main mathematical object is a linear transform: each output value is made by adding and subtracting selected input values according to a fixed pattern. In ordinary terms, it is like remixing a set of measurements so the same information is still present, but the values are spread differently. The Hadamard Transform is special because its pattern is recursive and uses only plus and minus signs. That matters for hardware because plus and minus are much cheaper than general multiplication. The second idea is quantization, which means replacing many possible real values with a small menu of representable levels. Quantization saves memory and arithmetic, but it loses detail when too many original values map to the same level. The transform is useful because it changes the shape of the input values before this rounding step, making the limited menu less unevenly used. The third idea is reduction: many small contributions are combined into a smaller number of accumulated results through a tree. Both Hadamard mixing and BitLinear accumulation reduce groups of values through repeated additions. The tradeoff is accuracy versus hardware cost: keep enough statistical spreading to avoid quantization collapse, while sharing physical adders so the cure does not become too expensive.
743.dots: This paper sits in the conference's efficiency and scalability thread, where systems cannot afford the direct version of the computation and must decide which work can be reused or moved closer to the data. It connects to quantized neural accelerators because the practical object is not merely a model layer, but a model layer mapped onto memory-side hardware. It also connects to information compression: quantization keeps only a small set of value levels, so the system must manage what detail is lost. The Hadamard step is a way of protecting useful signal before that compression happens. A neighboring idea is systems math, where the scarce resource is data movement, circuit area, power, or time rather than labeled data. Unlike retrieval or recommendation papers that save work by pruning candidates, this paper saves work by recognizing that two arithmetic tasks share the same reduction shape. The abstract supports a narrow but important claim: mathematical structure can guide physical circuit reuse.
743.ww: The mechanism should work because the added transform and the original bit-wise layer have a real structural overlap. If the Hadamard stage needed arbitrary multiplications, arbitrary routing, or a completely different memory access pattern, circuit reuse would be mostly cosmetic. But the abstract says the recursion can be expressed as linear combinations with weights from {-1, 0, 1}. That means each local operation is close to what an adder tree already does: pass a value, flip its sign, skip it, or add it into a running sum. The butterfly layout also matches a staged reduction process, where local pairwise combinations build larger combined results. Reusing this tree reduces duplicated datapaths and avoids moving transformed data through a separate block before accumulation. At the model level, the Hadamard Transform helps because it flattens inputs whose standard-normal concentration would otherwise waste quantization bins. At the hardware level, the unified datapath helps because it makes that accuracy-protecting transform cheaper to integrate into processing-in-memory.
743.po: The payoff is a BitNetv2-oriented processing-in-memory accelerator that can support both the Hadamard Transform and BitLinear bit-wise accumulation without treating them as unrelated operations. That buys a more practical route for matmul-free language-model layers: the quantization fix that protects accuracy is brought into the accelerator instead of being left as an expensive pre-processing step. The claimed benefit is reduced data-movement overhead through a unified reduction datapath, plus more efficient integration of Hadamard computation into memory-side hardware. In plain terms, the design tries to keep the accuracy advantage of better input statistics while preserving the speed and energy reason for using bit-wise PIM.
743.limits: The abstract describes the architectural idea but does not prove every deployment detail. The benefit depends on the model actually needing the BitNetv2-style Hadamard step and on the inputs having the concentration problem described in the paper. It also depends on the Hadamard and BitLinear schedules fitting the same butterfly adder-tree resources without causing stalls, routing pressure, or memory-bank conflicts that erase the savings. The abstract says the design aims to reduce data movement, but it does not give the measured area, power, latency, accuracy, or throughput numbers here. It also does not show how broadly the circuit applies beyond the specific matmul-free, bit-wise, low-precision setting.

744.bp: An e-commerce search box sits between a shopper's messy words and a catalog written in seller language. A buyer may type a short phrase, a nickname, a purpose, a misspelling, or a vague need; product pages may use brand terms, model numbers, materials, or professional descriptions. Query rewriting is the act of turning the shopper's original wording into a form that the search engine can match against products without losing what the shopper meant. This paper serves that practical moment: if the rewrite is too literal, useful products stay hidden; if it is too creative, the system may search for something the person did not ask for. The paper argues that current language-model rewriting methods often treat every query as if it had the same kind of problem. AWHCP instead asks what is wrong with this particular query, what intention lies behind it, what fix is needed, and what rewritten query should result.
744.wh: The hard part is that a bad query is not bad in one uniform way. One query may use different words from the catalog but still be clear. Another may be ambiguous. Another may contain a small spelling or wording issue. Another may need a rewrite that keeps the shopper's intent while making the product match easier. A system that handles all queries with one general rewriting habit can sound fluent while drifting away from what humans expect. The search engine also has two masters. It wants rewrites that retrieve better products, but shoppers want rewrites that feel like faithful interpretations of their own intent. These goals can conflict. A rewrite that helps the retrieval system may add product terms that a person did not imply. A rewrite that sounds human may fail to bridge the catalog wording gap. The paper's difficulty is therefore not only producing text, but deciding how hard the query is and what kind of linguistic repair it needs.
744.naive: A smart beginner would collect many query and product examples, train a large language model to rewrite every incoming query, and rank the produced rewrites by whether they seem to retrieve products well. That can help when the problem is a simple word mismatch. It fails when the model has no explicit habit of diagnosing the query first. The same rewriting strength may be applied to an easy query and a difficult one. The model may expand a clear query unnecessarily, overcorrect a harmless phrase, or invent a catalog-friendly phrase that changes the shopper's meaning. It also treats human preference as an afterthought: the rewrite may be valid text and useful to the system while still looking unlike the change a person would have made.
744.ap: The core idea is to make rewriting a visible reasoning chain rather than a single jump from old query to new query. The paper introduces a Problem-Intention-Fix-Rewrite structure. In plain terms, the model first learns to name the query's issue, then state the likely shopping intention, then decide the type of repair, and only then produce the rewritten query. AWHCP builds training data in that structure, so the model sees human-like rewriting behavior as a sequence of small decisions. It then aligns the model at more than one granularity. Coarsely, it generates several candidate rewrites and uses search-system feedback to prefer candidates that work better for retrieval. More finely, it trains a quality judge over multiple dimensions of rewrite quality and uses that judge to tune preferences closer to nuanced human expectations. The central move is difficulty-aware repair: different query problems receive different kinds of fixes.
744.mech: The mechanism starts with an e-commerce query and the surrounding evidence available from rewritten-query data and system feedback. First, the authors construct high-quality examples organized as Problem, Intention, Fix, and Rewrite. Each example does more than show the final answer; it records the path from a flawed or incomplete query to the intended repair. The model is then supervised on these examples, meaning it learns from direct demonstrations of how humans decompose rewriting decisions. Next, for a new or training query, the model does not keep only one rewrite. Beam search keeps several likely candidates, like asking the system to preserve a small shortlist of plausible repairs instead of committing too early. Those candidates can be compared using system-side feedback signals, so the model learns a coarse preference: among several possible rewrites, prefer the one that better serves retrieval. Finally, AWHCP adds a multi-dimensional rewrite quality judgment model. This judge is trained with Group Relative Policy Optimization, which can be understood as comparing candidates within a group and nudging the generator toward candidates judged better on several quality dimensions. The output is a rewrite process that carries an internal diagnosis, candidate generation, coarse system preference, fine human preference, and a final rewritten query meant to match both products and people.
744.math: Several mathematical ideas are doing ordinary work here. Learning from examples means finding a reusable mapping from one kind of object to another: from a raw shopper query to a diagnosis, intention, fix, and rewrite. The model changes its internal settings so that, across many examples, its produced steps resemble the human-provided steps. Candidate search is the second idea. Instead of assuming the first generated rewrite is best, beam search keeps multiple high-scoring options, preserving alternatives when language is uncertain. Preference learning is the third idea. The system compares candidate rewrites and asks which one should be preferred, not merely whether one exact answer was copied. Coarse direct preference alignment uses retrieval feedback as a signal about what helps the search engine. Fine-grained alignment uses a learned quality judge to score subtler human-facing properties. Group Relative Policy Optimization is an adjustment rule: candidates in the same group are compared, and the generator is pushed toward the ones that score better relative to their peers. The tradeoff is retrieval fit versus human faithfulness. The math fits because rewriting is not a yes-or-no classification; it is choosing among several plausible word changes under uncertainty about user intent and product matching.
744.dots: This paper belongs to the advertising and e-commerce family because it repairs the meaning channel before a marketplace ranking decision is made. Many commerce papers in the repo handle the later choice: which product, ad, price, coupon, or page element should be shown when attention is scarce. AWHCP works one step earlier. It asks whether the shopper's words have been translated into a search form that preserves intent. It also connects to the ranking concept because beam search and preference alignment both turn several candidates into an order: this rewrite is better than that one for the current goal. It connects to matching because the final purpose is to pair a query with products whose descriptions may use different language. The language-model part links it to broader WWW 2026 work where large language models are used as interpreters and assistants, not just answer generators. The shared conference pressure is the same: logged behavior, human intention, and system objectives only partly agree, so the method must make that disagreement explicit.
744.ww: The method should improve over uniform rewriting because it separates problems that would otherwise be blended together. If a query only needs a small wording bridge, the Problem-Intention-Fix-Rewrite path can teach the model not to overexpand it. If a query has a deeper mismatch with catalog language, the same path can justify a stronger repair. The first supervised stage gives the model human demonstrations of how rewriting decisions are decomposed. That matters because the final rewrite is easier to trust when it follows from an identified problem and intention. The beam-search stage helps because language generation is uncertain: several rewrites may be plausible, and keeping candidates allows the system to compare them rather than accept the first fluent one. System feedback keeps the rewrite tied to retrieval usefulness, while the quality judge keeps it tied to human rewriting preference. The approach works if these signals correct different errors: retrieval feedback catches product-matching failures, and human-oriented quality judgment catches rewrites that drift from what a shopper would expect.
744.po: The payoff is a query rewriting system that treats e-commerce search as a human interpretation problem, not only a text generation problem. According to the abstract, AWHCP was deployed on 1688's main search engine starting in August 2025. The authors report extensive offline evaluation, large-scale online A/B tests, and a 3.9 percent gain in UV-L2O. The abstract does not define UV-L2O, but within the search-engine setting it is presented as an online business or user-behavior metric improved by better rewriting. The practical capability is difficulty-aware rewriting: the system can produce rewrites that are meant to retrieve better products while staying closer to human cognition and preference.
744.limits: The claims depend on the constructed PIFR data being high quality and representative of real shopper language. If the examples encode narrow annotator habits, the model may learn those habits rather than general human cognition. System-side feedback is also shaped by the current search engine, catalog, ranking rules, and user base, so a rewrite that helps 1688 may not transfer unchanged to another marketplace. The quality judge can only reward dimensions it has learned to measure. The abstract reports deployment and A/B gains, but it does not prove which query types improved, where rewrites still drift from intent, how the system behaves under rare or adversarial queries, or whether long-term seller and buyer effects remain positive.

745.bp: A table is not just a short document. It is a grid where meaning is spread across column names, row values, repeated patterns, and the relations among cells. A person may ask, "Which table could answer this question?" while the table itself may never contain that question in sentence form. Table retrieval is the job of finding the right table from a large collection when the request is written like prose and the evidence is stored as rows and columns. CGPT serves systems such as question answering over web tables, enterprise data lakes, and table search, where the first failure is often upstream: the useful table never reaches the later answering step. The paper starts from the observation that general text-search numeric fingerprints work well for ordinary passages but lose too much when a table is squeezed into one short description. CGPT tries to teach the search model what table questions sound like and which table fragments should answer them.
745.wh: The hard part is that table meaning is compressed by structure. A cell value such as "France" or "2018" may be meaningful only because of its column header, neighboring rows, and the table topic. If the whole table is flattened into text, many local meanings collide, and the searchable fingerprint can become a vague average. That causes query-table mismatch: the user's wording points to an intended fact, but the table's stored form points to a grid layout rather than a sentence. Recent methods ask a language model to invent likely queries for tables, which helps translate grid evidence into user-like wording. But the abstract says those methods often choose partial tables by heuristic rules, meaning fixed or hand-designed shortcuts. If the chosen fragment is repetitive or unrepresentative, the generated questions train the model on a narrow view of the table. They also may not be used strongly enough to improve the fingerprint model itself.
745.naive: A smart beginner would serialize each table into text, run a strong general-purpose text retriever, and rank tables by closeness to the user's query. If that underperforms, the next beginner move would be to sample a few rows or columns, ask a language model to write questions for those snippets, and add those questions as extra searchable text. This fails because the sample can miss the table's internal variety. A large table may contain several groups of rows with different meanings, and random or fixed partial-table selection can overrepresent common-looking rows. The generated queries then describe what happened to be selected, not the broader set of things the table can answer. The retriever learns a shallow translation rather than a better table-aware comparison rule.
745.ap: CGPT's central move is to make the training examples cover different semantic regions of the table before asking a language model for supervision. It first clusters table instances with K-means, a procedure that groups items around learned centers according to numeric closeness. Then it samples across those groups so the partial tables are semantically diverse rather than chosen by a simple rule. A language model writes synthetic queries for these selected partial tables, turning structured snippets into the kinds of requests a user might type. Those generated query-table pairs become training supervision for the retriever. The model is fine-tuned with hard-negative contrastive training: it is shown a matching query and table, along with confusing nonmatching tables, and it is trained to pull the match closer while pushing the near-misses apart. The idea is not merely to decorate tables with generated text, but to change the search model's notion of table-query closeness.
745.mech: The mechanism begins with a table collection and a retrieval model that already turns queries and tables into compact numeric fingerprints for comparison. CGPT first needs better table fragments. Instead of picking partial tables by a fixed recipe, it represents table instances in a way that allows them to be compared, then runs K-means clustering. K-means repeatedly assigns each instance to the nearest center and moves each center toward the average of what it owns; the result is a set of groups that roughly cover different regions of table meaning. CGPT samples across these groups so the partial tables given to the language model are not all variants of the same local pattern. Next, the language model generates synthetic queries for those partial tables. Each generated query is treated as a plausible user request whose answer or evidence is the corresponding table fragment. The training stage then forms positive pairs, where the query and its source table should be close, and hard negative pairs, where another table is plausible enough to confuse the retriever but should not win. Fine-tuning adjusts the retrieval model so the score for the true query-table pair rises above the scores for the confusing alternatives. At search time, a real user query is converted into the same comparison form, candidate tables are scored, and the output is a ranked list where the relevant table is intended to appear near the top.
745.math: The mathematical ideas are similarity, clustering, ranking, and contrastive learning. Similarity means choosing which differences matter when two unlike objects, a prose query and a table, must be compared. The model represents each object as a list of numbers, a compact fingerprint, so distance or score can stand in for relatedness. The danger is compression: a table with many row groups can be squeezed into a single bland location. Clustering addresses that by looking for groups before supervision is generated. In K-means, centers are placed in the comparison space, items join the nearest center, and the centers move toward their assigned items until the groups stabilize. This is a way of saying, "do not sample only from the crowded middle; cover several neighborhoods." Contrastive learning is comparison-based training. It does not merely ask whether one pair is good; it asks the model to put the true pair closer than difficult wrong pairs. Hard negatives matter because easy wrong tables teach little. Ranking is the final mathematical object: tables are sorted by scores, and the top position matters because the abstract reports R@1, whether the first retrieved table is the right one. The tradeoff is coverage versus noise: more diverse generated supervision can teach broader table meaning, but only if the generated queries really describe the selected fragments.
745.dots: This paper belongs to the repo's information-retrieval, similarity, ranking, and language-model supervision threads. Like other retrieval papers, it must choose a small useful set from a large pile before any later reasoning can happen. It is close to the table-retrieval siblings already present in the data. STAR also focuses on the representation bottleneck in table search, using cluster-guided partial evidence and generated queries so a table's many meanings are not collapsed into one weak summary. GeCo-TR attacks a related cold-start problem by modeling table structure and linked knowledge-graph evidence when query-level labels are unavailable. FollowTable shifts the pressure toward instruction following, where a table must satisfy explicit content and schema constraints rather than match only a topic. CGPT's branch is the supervision branch: it uses a language model to create query examples, then uses those examples to retrain the table-query comparison map. Across these papers, the deeper shared problem is that tables speak in structure while users and agents ask in language.
745.ww: CGPT should improve over the naive approach because it fixes two linked bottlenecks. First, clustering before partial-table construction gives the language model a wider diet of table evidence. If generated queries are based only on arbitrary fragments, the training signal can repeat common rows and ignore rarer table regions. Sampling across clusters makes it more likely that different column-row patterns produce different query examples. Second, hard-negative contrastive fine-tuning turns those examples into pressure on the retriever itself. A generated query is not just appended as text; it becomes a lesson about what should be closer and what should remain separate. The hard negatives are important because table retrieval errors often involve near matches: two tables may share surface words but answer different questions because their structure differs. Training against these confusing alternatives teaches the model to notice distinctions that ordinary text retrieval may smooth away. The abstract's cross-domain result also fits this intuition. If supervision covers diverse table meanings rather than one dataset's repeated wording, the learned comparison rule has a better chance of transferring to new table domains.
745.po: The payoff is a table retriever whose top result is more often the right table. The abstract reports experiments on MimoTable, OTTQA, FetaQA, and E2E-WTQ, with CGPT outperforming baselines by an average R@1 improvement of 16.54%. In practical terms, that means the first table shown to a user or downstream answering system is more likely to be useful. The abstract also says CGPT works in cross-domain evaluation and remains effective with smaller language models for query generation. That matters because table search is often needed across collections where labeled query-table pairs are scarce and expensive to gather.
745.limits: The claims depend on the generated queries being faithful to the partial tables. If the language model writes fluent but inaccurate or overly generic questions, the retriever can learn the wrong closeness rule. The method also assumes the initial table representations used for K-means are good enough for clusters to reflect meaningful diversity. If that first map is poor, sampling across clusters may only create the appearance of coverage. The abstract reports four public benchmarks and cross-domain evaluation, but it does not prove behavior on every table style, noisy enterprise schema, rare language, or instruction-heavy request. It also does not show whether synthetic supervision introduces systematic biases from the query generator.

746.bp: A traffic service is trying to answer a simple practical question: how crowded will each road segment be soon enough for a route planner or remote traffic manager to act? The usual evidence is a record of earlier speeds or flows at each place. That evidence matters, because rush hour, weekends, and repeated bottlenecks leave patterns in time. But a road is not just a column of past numbers. It sits inside a physical layout, near intersections, bridges, neighborhoods, event sites, and alternative routes. Some of that context is visible in web-sourced geo-images such as satellite imagery. VisionST serves the need to combine these different forms of evidence. The paper asks traffic prediction to look not only backward in the traffic log, but also outward at the place where the traffic happens, so future flow can be predicted with richer knowledge of the road network and surrounding context.
746.wh: The hard part is that traffic changes for more than one reason at once. A road may slow because it is historically busy at that hour, because nearby roads feed cars into it, because its physical layout creates a chokepoint, or because a social event changes demand. These causes do not arrive in the same format. Historical traffic is a sequence of numbers over time. The road system is a set of connected places. A satellite image is a picture whose useful clues must be found before they can guide prediction. A model that studies only one source can mistake a regular time pattern for a place-specific pattern, or miss why two nearby roads influence each other differently. The abstract also stresses intricate and overlapping traffic patterns, meaning that several explanations can be true together. The challenge is not merely adding images; it is making visual, spatial, and temporal evidence interact in a controlled way.
746.naive: A smart beginner would collect recent traffic readings for every road node and train a predictor to extend each sequence into the future. They might also add a simple road-neighbor rule: nearby or connected roads should influence one another. This works for repeated daily patterns, but it treats the physical world as if it were already fully encoded in the past traffic log. It misses context that has not appeared often enough in the numbers, such as a road shape, surrounding land use, or event-related area. Another beginner fix would attach one image feature to each road and let the model use it as extra input. That still fails if the useful visual clue is relational, for example when the image says two nodes share a corridor-like relation rather than just separate local appearances.
746.ap: VisionST's central move is to turn geo-referenced images into traffic-specific relational evidence, then use that evidence to guide how road nodes exchange information. It does not treat the satellite image as decoration or as one extra static label. The visual semantic extraction mechanism reads the image around the traffic network and produces two kinds of clues: node-level visual tokens, meaning compact pieces of image information tied to individual road nodes, and node-to-node visual relation patterns, meaning image-derived clues about how two places may be related. The pattern-guided aggregation mechanism then forms relation patterns that include visual, spatial, and temporal aspects. In plain terms, it gives each road node a structured way to listen to other nodes: not just because they are connected, and not just because their past traffic looks similar, but because image context, road position, and time behavior jointly suggest a useful interaction.
746.mech: The input is a traffic network observed over time, plus geo-referenced images such as satellite imagery aligned with the places in that network. First, the system represents each road location or sensor as a node whose past traffic readings provide the temporal signal. Second, the visual semantic extraction part examines the corresponding image evidence. It extracts node-level visual tokens, which are small summaries of what the image says about a particular node, and it also extracts visual relation patterns between nodes. Here, token just means a compact piece of information the model can move around, not a word. Third, the model builds relation patterns that combine three views: visual context from the image, spatial context from where roads or nodes sit relative to one another, and temporal context from how traffic has changed over time. Fourth, pattern-guided aggregation uses these relation patterns to constrain how nodes interact. A node does not blindly average all neighbors. It receives contextual information through the relation patterns judged relevant by the combined visual, spatial, and temporal evidence. Finally, the spatial-temporal neural network uses the resulting node states to output future traffic predictions. The abstract reports extensive experiments on real large-scale datasets and says VisionST consistently outperforms prior baselines.
746.math: The main mathematical object is a changing network. Nodes stand for traffic locations, links or relations stand for ways one location can inform another, and each node carries a time sequence of traffic observations. The paper adds image-derived evidence to that network. One mathematical idea is representation: turning a complicated object, such as a satellite image patch, into a compact set of numbers that preserves traffic-relevant clues while discarding many visual details. Another is relational scoring: deciding which node-to-node interactions deserve weight because visual, spatial, and temporal evidence agree that they matter. A third is aggregation, which means collecting information from other nodes after deciding how much each relation should count. The tradeoff is local evidence versus broader context. Looking only at one road is too narrow; mixing every road equally spreads noise. VisionST's pattern-guided aggregation is a middle path: it defines relation patterns that tell the model where evidence should travel. The learning part is an error-reduction process: predictions are compared with observed future traffic, and the model's internal settings are adjusted so future errors shrink on the training data. The abstract does not give equations, so the exact scoring formulas cannot be reconstructed from the input alone.
746.dots: This paper belongs to the conference's time-series and spatiotemporal thread because it predicts a quantity that changes over time and depends on location. It is a sibling of other traffic and spatiotemporal work that asks how evidence should move across roads, sensors, services, or cities without assuming every channel behaves the same. It also sits in the multimodal thread, where the key pressure is that one data type is too poor a witness: text, images, tables, graphs, or time series each reveal only part of the situation. VisionST's version of that pressure is concrete. Historical traffic tells what happened; satellite imagery can show physical and contextual conditions under which it happened. The paper also connects to graph reasoning, because nodes exchange information through learned relation patterns, and to similarity/ranking ideas, because the system must implicitly decide which other nodes are relevant enough to influence a prediction.
746.ww: The intuitive reason VisionST can beat a history-only predictor is that traffic has stable causes that are not always visible in the traffic numbers themselves. A road segment near a dense intersection, a highway ramp, or an event-heavy area may repeatedly behave differently from a visually different segment with a similar recent traffic curve. If the model can read such place context from geo-images, it has another way to separate cases that look alike in short history but are likely to evolve differently. The node-to-node visual relations matter for the same reason. Two roads may influence each other not just because they are geographically close, but because their visual and network context suggests a shared flow pattern. Pattern-guided aggregation helps by restricting information exchange to relations supported by multiple clues. That can reduce the common failure where a model either ignores useful neighboring context or mixes in too much irrelevant neighboring noise. The mechanism works if the image features really capture traffic-relevant context and align correctly with the road nodes.
746.po: The payoff is a traffic predictor that can use web-sourced geo-images as context rather than relying only on past traffic observations. For route planning, that means the service can make forecasts informed by the road's visible surroundings and by relations among road nodes. For remote traffic management, it offers a richer warning signal about future congestion because visual, spatial, and temporal evidence are considered together. The abstract grounds the result in real large-scale datasets and reports that VisionST consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. The practical gain is not simply a higher score; it is fewer missed traffic patterns when the relevant cause is partly outside the raw traffic history.
746.limits: Several assumptions must hold. The geo-images must be correctly matched to the traffic nodes, and the visual clues in those images must be relevant to future traffic rather than incidental scenery. Satellite imagery may show road layout and surroundings, but it may not show temporary social events unless their locations have stable visual markers. The method also assumes that learned node-to-node visual relation patterns transfer from past data to future conditions. If road usage changes, sensors move, construction alters the network, or events create patterns not represented in training, the image-guided relations may mislead. The abstract reports large-scale experiments and consistent gains, but it does not prove which visual cues the model uses, how it behaves under rare disruptions, or how costly the image processing is in deployment.

747.bp: The real object in this paper is a web graph where each node is a person, account, page, transaction, product, device, or other entity, and some nodes behave unlike the rest. In high-stakes web settings, those abnormal nodes may stand for fraud, abuse, failures, or rare harmful activity. Graph anomaly detection tries to notice them by looking at both what a node is and how it sits among neighbors. The practical problem is that most graph anomaly detectors are built one graph at a time. A model trained for one network may not work on another, because the node features, link patterns, and kinds of abnormal behavior change. TFM4GAD asks whether a model originally built for tables can become a reusable graph anomaly detector. The paper's larger purpose is to reduce retraining, data hunger, and poor transfer across diverse graphs.
747.wh: The hard part is that graphs differ in two ways at once. First, their rows of facts differ: one graph may describe accounts with activity counts, another may describe products, pages, or transactions with different attributes. Second, their structure differs: some graphs are dense, some sparse, some have communities, some have hubs, and anomalies may be unusual because of their features, their neighborhoods, or the mismatch between the two. A detector trained from scratch on each dataset can adapt to those local quirks, but that is expensive and needs enough labels. A reusable model has the opposite problem: it must transfer without assuming that every new graph has the same shape. Tabular foundation models are attractive because they are trained to handle many table-like feature patterns and learn from examples placed in the prompt context, but they do not naturally know that graph links carry information.
747.naive: A smart beginner would train a separate graph anomaly model for every new dataset. They would feed in the node features, use the graph edges to mix information from neighbors, and learn which nodes look abnormal from the available labels. That can work when labels are plentiful and the next graph resembles the training graph. It fails as a general solution because every domain forces the model to relearn local feature meanings and structural habits. Another beginner might simply ignore the graph and put raw node features into a table model. That saves retraining, but it throws away the main reason the data was a graph: suspiciousness can live in who a node connects to, how isolated it is, or how unlike its neighbors it appears.
747.ap: The core idea is translation. Instead of forcing a tabular foundation model to read edges directly, TFM4GAD turns each node into a richer table row. The row keeps the node's original attributes, then adds numbers that summarize the node's position and neighborhood in the graph. Laplacian position features, meaning numeric coordinates derived from the graph's connection pattern, give the table model a sense of where a node sits in the network. Local and global structural characteristics describe nearby and whole-graph shape. Anomaly-sensitive neighborhood aggregations summarize what the node's neighbors look like in ways useful for spotting abnormality. Once the graph has been flattened into this augmented table, the tabular model can operate fully through in-context learning, meaning it uses examples supplied at prediction time instead of being retrained for that dataset.
747.mech: The mechanism begins with a graph: nodes, node features, edges, and usually scarce labels indicating which nodes are known to be normal or abnormal. First, TFM4GAD keeps the raw node features because many anomalies are visible as strange attribute combinations. Second, it computes Laplacian position features from the graph's link structure. These features compress connection patterns into numeric coordinates, so two nodes with different structural roles can look different even if their raw attributes are similar. Third, it adds local and global structural characteristics, such as summaries of how a node is connected nearby and how it relates to the broader graph. Fourth, it builds anomaly-sensitive neighborhood aggregations: instead of looking only at a node alone, it summarizes neighbor information because abnormal nodes often reveal themselves by disagreeing with their surroundings. These pieces are concatenated into an augmented feature table, one row per node. The tabular foundation model receives that table and a small set of labeled examples in context. It compares rows through their combined attribute and structural evidence, scores which unlabeled nodes look unlike the normal pattern, and outputs anomaly predictions without training a new graph-specific model from scratch.
747.math: Three mathematical ideas matter here. The first is turning relationships into measurements. A graph is not naturally a table because an edge is a relation between two nodes, not a value stored inside one row. Laplacian position features solve part of that by using the pattern of connections to assign each node numeric coordinates. In everyday terms, the graph's shape is converted into address-like numbers. The second idea is summarization. Local and global structural statistics compress a node's neighborhood and graph role into values a table model can read. This is useful, but it loses detail: two different neighborhoods can share the same summary. The third idea is combining weak signals. Raw attributes, position features, structural summaries, and neighbor aggregates are each incomplete clues. An anomaly score becomes more trustworthy when several clues point to the same node. The tradeoff is structure versus transfer. A specialized graph model can reason directly over links but may not transfer; a tabular model transfers better across feature types, but only after graph structure has been translated into row-level numbers the model can compare.
747.dots: This paper sits in the fraud and anomaly detection family because it asks how to spot rare, risky cases when examples are scarce and the setting changes. It connects to graph-learning work through the assumption that links are evidence: neighbors, positions, hubs, and communities help decide whether a node is ordinary or suspicious. It also connects to foundation-model work because the goal is a one-for-all detector rather than a new model per dataset. The repo's math tags for this paper point to similarity, relevance weighting, and combining weak signals. Those ideas appear here as row comparison, deciding which structural summaries matter, and merging many small pieces of evidence into one anomaly judgment. Compared with video or text anomaly papers, this one changes the surface object, but the deeper problem is shared: abnormality is not a fixed label pattern. It is deviation from what counts as normal in a specific context.
747.ww: The method should help because it gives each side of the problem to the tool that is better suited for it. Tabular foundation models are designed to handle many kinds of columns, mixed feature meanings, and small in-context examples. That matches the cross-domain part of graph anomaly detection: a new graph may arrive with unfamiliar attributes and few labels. Graph structure is the missing ingredient, so TFM4GAD does not ask the tabular model to infer edges from nowhere. It precomputes structural evidence and places it beside the raw features. If anomalies often appear as unusual combinations, then a node's table row should expose those combinations: odd attributes, odd position, odd neighborhood, or a mismatch among them. This can outperform one-model-per-dataset methods when those specialized models overfit to one graph's quirks or require more labeled data than the new graph provides. The approach works best when the flattened features preserve enough of the graph's abnormality signal.
747.po: The payoff is a practical route to reusable graph anomaly detection. According to the abstract, TFM4GAD operates across diverse graphs without retraining, uses tabular foundation models in a fully in-context regime, and achieves significant gains over specialized graph anomaly detectors trained from scratch across multiple datasets and several tabular-model backbones. The capability is not merely a higher score. It is the ability to take a new graph, convert each node into an augmented table row containing both attribute and structural evidence, and ask a pre-trained table model to identify abnormal nodes with scarce labels and lower retraining cost.
747.limits: The approach assumes that graph structure can be flattened into table columns without losing the distinctions needed to catch anomalies. That may fail when the abnormal pattern depends on long chains, motifs, temporal behavior, or edge semantics that simple summaries do not preserve. It also depends on the tabular foundation model's pre-training and in-context behavior transferring to the new graph's feature types. The abstract reports experiments on multiple datasets and backbones, but it does not prove the method works for every web domain, every anomaly type, adversarially hidden anomalies, changing graphs, or settings where labels are biased. The table translation is powerful, but it is still a compressed view of the graph.

748.bp: Online moderation systems are asked to make judgments that affect whose speech is removed, flagged, or left alone. Toxicity assessment is one version of that job: the system reads a post and decides whether it contains abuse, hate, or harmful language. Large language models, meaning text models trained to predict and respond to language, are attractive here because they can read subtle wording better than a simple banned-word list. But the decision is not only about accuracy. If the model judges language tied to one demographic group more harshly than similar language tied to another group, the moderation system becomes unfair even when it sounds consistent. This paper serves the practical problem of making model-based toxicity judgments fairer at decision time. Its key question is not just how to correct a model, but when a correction should be invoked, especially for implicit hate speech and subtle expressions where unfair variation is most likely.
748.wh: The hard part is that toxic meaning is often indirect. A post may avoid obvious slurs while still targeting a group, or it may mention a demographic group in a harmless, reclaimed, quoted, or critical context. A model has to judge both the words and the social situation those words imply. Bias enters because the model has learned from many past examples where demographic terms, insults, stereotypes, and moderation labels were mixed together in uneven ways. Standard training can reduce some visible errors, but the abstract says inconsistent judgments remain, especially for subtle expressions. A second difficulty is cost and stability. If every moderation decision is sent through a heavy corrective process, the system may become slower and may disturb judgments that were already reliable. If correction is never applied, unfair group-level disparities remain. The central tension is therefore selective intervention: detect the cases where demographic-related variation is likely before deciding whether extra assessment is worth applying.
748.naive: A smart beginner might try two simple fixes. The first is to ask the language model for a toxicity score once and trust the answer. That fails because the abstract says the same kind of subtle expression can receive inconsistent judgments, especially when demographic cues are involved. The second is to apply a fairness correction to every input. That sounds safer, but it treats clear cases and uncertain cases as if they had the same risk. It may add cost, change stable decisions unnecessarily, and still not explain why some inputs needed extra scrutiny. The missing piece is a trigger: a way to recognize when the ordinary judgment is likely to vary across demographic framing and therefore deserves a more careful pass.
748.ap: The paper's core move is to place a guard before the correction. FairToT works at inference time, meaning after the model has already been trained and while it is answering a particular moderation request. Instead of changing the model's internal parameters, it uses prompt-guided toxicity assessment and interpretable fairness indicators to decide whether a case is at risk of demographic-related variation. In concrete terms, the system first asks whether the current text is the kind of example where group identity may alter the model's judgment. If the indicators suggest that unfair variation is likely, the system invokes additional assessment. If not, it can leave the ordinary judgment alone. This turns fairness improvement from a blanket retraining problem into a routing problem: send the fragile cases through extra checking, while preserving stable predictions where the model appears less likely to produce group-dependent inconsistency.
748.mech: The input is a piece of text that an online moderation system wants to judge for toxicity. The base language model can already produce a toxicity assessment, but FairToT adds a decision layer around that assessment. First, the system examines the case through prompt-guided questions rather than relying only on the original answer. These prompts are not described in full in the abstract, so the safe inference is that they ask the model to evaluate toxicity in a way that exposes whether demographic wording is influencing the judgment. Second, FairToT computes two interpretable fairness indicators. The abstract does not name their exact formulas, but it does state their role: they detect cases where demographic-related variation is likely to occur. The indicators therefore act like warning lights, converting a hidden risk of unfair variation into a visible signal. Third, the system decides whether to invoke additional assessment. For flagged cases, the model receives extra prompt-guided scrutiny intended to make the toxicity decision more consistent across demographic groups. For unflagged cases, the system avoids unnecessary intervention. The output is still a toxicity prediction for the moderation system, but it is produced by a conditional process: ordinary assessment for lower-risk cases and refined assessment for cases where demographic sensitivity appears likely. The reported experiments compare this process on benchmark datasets and measure whether group-level disparities fall while prediction stability remains.
748.math: The main mathematical idea is estimating uncertainty and unfair variation from observable signals. A toxicity model gives judgments, but fairness asks a second question: do those judgments change in a patterned way when demographic group information is involved? That is a comparison problem. The system needs to compare assessments across cases or prompt conditions and decide whether the difference is large enough to suggest demographic-related variation rather than ordinary noise. The fairness indicators are measurement rules. A measurement rule takes messy behavior, such as inconsistent model answers, and turns it into a number or label that can guide action. This fits the paper because unfairness is not directly visible inside the model; it has to be inferred from how judgments behave. There is also a routing idea. The system sorts inputs into those needing extra assessment and those that do not, which is a constrained decision because extra checking has cost and may disturb stable outputs. Prompt-guided assessment uses the model as a repeated judge under controlled wording. The mathematical risk is false confidence: an indicator may miss a biased case, or it may flag a harmless case. The tradeoff is fairness versus intervention cost, and consistency versus overcorrection. FairToT's contribution is to make that tradeoff explicit at inference time instead of hiding it inside retraining.
748.dots: This paper connects to the repo's fairness and responsible-AI thread because a toxicity score is not just a prediction; it allocates moderation pressure across speakers and communities. It also connects to the language-model and prompt-guidance thread, where researchers try to steer a trained model's behavior without changing its internal parameters. The closest recurring idea is selective escalation. Other moderation and live-understanding papers in the repo ask when cheap local evidence is enough and when a stronger assessment should be called. FairToT applies that same shape to demographic fairness: the hard question is when to invoke extra scrutiny. It also touches causality in a modest sense. The system is concerned with whether demographic-related wording is associated with a changed judgment, while the abstract does not claim a full causal proof of why the bias arose. Compared with retrieval or recommendation fairness work, the item being ranked is absent; here the fairness pressure falls on a classifier whose output may remove or preserve speech.
748.ww: FairToT should improve over the naive approach because it matches the correction to the failure pattern described in the abstract. If biased inconsistency is concentrated in subtle expressions and implicit hate speech, then a global correction is a blunt tool. It spends effort on easy cases and can introduce new instability. A trigger-based method instead asks where the ordinary answer is likely to be fragile. The fairness indicators help because they give the system an intermediate observable target: not merely whether the text is toxic, but whether the judgment is likely to vary with demographic framing. That extra target matters because a model can be confidently wrong or inconsistently sensitive in ways that a single toxicity score hides. Prompt-guided reassessment then gives the model another structured chance to separate harmful intent from demographic mention. Because this happens without parameter changes, it can be added to an existing moderation pipeline more practically than retraining. The reported result, reduced group-level disparities while maintaining stable predictions, is exactly what this mechanism is designed to buy: less unfair variation without turning every answer into a moving target.
748.po: The payoff is a more practical fairness layer for language-model toxicity assessment. The system can improve fairness at the moment a moderation decision is made, without retraining the model or modifying its parameters. According to the abstract, FairToT reduces group-level disparities on benchmark datasets while keeping toxicity predictions stable and reliable. For a moderation team, the useful capability is conditional care: identify cases where demographic-related variation is likely, apply additional prompt-guided assessment there, and avoid needless correction elsewhere. That makes fairness refinement operational rather than only a training-time research exercise.
748.limits: The claims depend on the fairness indicators actually detecting the cases where demographic-related variation matters. If the indicators miss coded language, local slang, reclaimed terms, or culturally specific insults, unfair judgments may remain. If they overflag, the system may spend extra assessment on cases that did not need it and may introduce new inconsistency. The abstract reports benchmark experiments, but it does not prove reliability across platforms, languages, moderation policies, or adversarial users who adapt their wording. It also does not describe the exact indicator formulas or prompts, so the transparency claim can only be accepted at the level stated: the indicators are interpretable, not fully specified here.

749.bp: Security video is useful only when it helps people understand a dangerous event fast enough to respond, review, or prevent a repeat. Older video anomaly systems mostly ask two questions: is something threatening in this clip, and where in the video does it happen? DeepSVU asks for a harder kind of help. If a segment shows a robbery, shooting, or other threat, the system should also explain the cause of the threatening segment and judge that explanation. The real object is not a single suspicious frame. It is a physical scene unfolding over time: people move, objects are handled, and the background gives meaning to those actions. A person raising an arm, a person near a counter, or a crowded room can each be harmless alone. Together, and in the right order, they may explain why a segment is dangerous. This paper serves security-oriented video understanding by turning detection into in-depth question answering about threats.
749.wh: The hard part is that threat causes live at several sizes at once. A coarse clue may be the general scene: street, store, hallway, crowd, or empty background. A finer clue may be one person's behavior or one object interaction. The cause of a threat is often in the relation between these clues, not in any clue by itself. A video system that sees only visual pattern may mark a segment as abnormal without being able to say whether the danger came from a weapon-like object, a sudden human action, or the surrounding context. A system that treats every physical clue equally also fails, because different events need different evidence. For one threat, human behavior may dominate. For another, the object interaction may be decisive. The paper identifies exactly this tension: model coarse-to-fine physical-world information and adaptively trade off behavior, object interaction, and background context.
749.naive: A smart beginner would first train a video anomaly detector to mark suspicious frames, then attach a short caption after the fact. That can locate unusual segments, but the explanation is weak because the detector was never forced to organize evidence around causes. Another beginner move is to build separate detectors for people, objects, and scenes, then average their outputs. Averaging breaks because it assumes the same evidence mix works for every threat. A raised hand, a carried object, and a dark background should not always receive equal influence. The simple system may notice danger while giving the wrong reason, or may miss danger because the strongest clue is diluted by many ordinary-looking details.
749.ap: The paper's central move is to make physical evidence part of the reasoning path instead of treating it as decoration after detection. Its UPRM approach, short for Unified Physical-world Regularized MoE, uses two named parts. The UPE block is meant to gather physical-world information across levels, from broad scene context down to human behavior and object interactions. MoE means mixture of experts: several specialist submodels each read the case in a different way, while a routing rule decides how much each specialist should influence the answer. PTR, the Physical-world Trade-off Regularizer, is the balancing pressure that discourages the system from leaning blindly on one factor. In concrete terms, DeepSVU asks the model to identify and locate threats, but also to attribute and evaluate the causes of threatening segments by weighing the right physical clues for each video.
749.mech: The input is a security video paired with instruction-style questions from the paper's DeepSVU datasets, UCF-C instructions and CUVA instructions. The system must produce chat-style answers about whether a threat appears, where the threatening segment is, what caused it, and how the cause should be evaluated. First, the video is divided into evidence that can be read at different physical scales. Broad background context tells what kind of place and situation the action occurs in. Human behavior evidence describes movements and poses. Object-interaction evidence describes how people and things affect one another. Next, the UPE block brings these levels into a unified representation, meaning a combined internal description that keeps them available for the same decision. The mixture-of-experts part then routes the current segment through specialists. One specialist may be more useful for body motion, another for objects, another for context, depending on the threat. The PTR component adds a rule during learning that pushes the system to manage tradeoffs among these physical factors instead of letting whichever signal is easiest in the training data dominate. The result is not just an anomaly score. It is an in-depth security-oriented answer: identify the threat, locate the relevant segment, attribute likely causes using physical-world evidence, and evaluate those causes.
749.math: The main mathematical idea is selective weighting under a constraint. Selective weighting starts from a simple fact: a video contains more evidence than can be trusted equally. The model breaks the scene into parts, gives different parts different amounts of influence, and combines them to form an answer. The mixture-of-experts structure is one way to do this. Each expert is a learned function, meaning a rule shaped from examples, that is better suited to some slice of evidence. A routing rule assigns weights to the experts for the current case. A high weight says this expert's view should count more; a low weight says it should mostly stay quiet. The regularizer is a mathematical penalty, a term added to the learning score to make some behavior costly. Here the abstract says the penalty is tied to physical-world tradeoffs, so its role is to make the learned routing respect behavior, object interaction, and background context instead of collapsing to a careless shortcut. The broader learning problem is also a scored search: define wrong answers as poor threat detection, poor localization, poor attribution, or poor cause evaluation, then adjust the model to reduce that wrongness. The tradeoff is focus versus blindness: stronger weighting can highlight the cause, but can also miss weak context.
749.dots: This paper belongs with anomaly-detection work because it asks when behavior stops fitting the ordinary scene, but it pushes beyond a binary alarm. It also belongs with multimodal and video-language papers because the output is chat-like understanding rather than only a class label, and the evidence must connect visual events to textual answers. Its closest recurring ideas are ranking, probability, selective weighting, and physical reasoning. Ranking appears when the system must decide which segment and which cause deserve priority. Probability appears implicitly because the model estimates which explanation is most plausible from partial video evidence. Selective weighting appears through the mixture-of-experts design: different clues speak more loudly in different threats. The broader conference connection is the move from recognition to explanation. Many 2026 papers ask systems not only to predict, retrieve, or flag, but to show which evidence carried the decision and when that evidence should be trusted.
749.ww: The approach should improve over a naive detector because causes in security video are often compositional. A threat can be caused by a person moving in a certain way, an object being used in a certain relation to that person, and a background that makes the action meaningful. If the model sees those physical pieces separately and then learns how to trade them off, it has a better chance of separating real causes from surface oddities. The mixture design helps because one universal reader may blur different threat types together. Robbery-like, shooting-like, and other abnormal events can demand different evidence balances. The regularizing pressure helps for a second reason: training data can reward shortcuts, such as always trusting background or always trusting motion. By making physical-world tradeoffs part of the learning objective, UPRM tries to keep the explanation tied to the scene's actual moving parts. That does not prove human-level causality, but it gives the model a more suitable language for cause attribution than a lone anomaly score.
749.po: The payoff is a more useful security-video assistant. According to the abstract, DeepSVU is designed to identify, locate, attribute, and evaluate anomalies in threatening videos, rather than stopping after detection. The paper reports extensive experiments on UCF-C instructions and CUVA instructions, where UPRM outperforms advanced video large language models and non-language-model approaches. The practical capability is richer review: an operator or downstream system can ask not only where the suspicious segment is, but which human behavior, object interaction, or background context made it threatening. That is a stronger basis for investigation than a timestamp alone.
749.limits: The claims depend on the DeepSVU instruction datasets representing the security situations people actually care about. If those instructions or videos overrepresent certain threat types, backgrounds, or camera views, the learned tradeoffs may not carry over. The abstract says the method attributes and evaluates causes, but it does not prove true causality in the human sense; it learns evidence patterns associated with causes in labeled examples. It also does not specify from the provided text how explanations are judged by human operators. The approach assumes physical cues are visible enough: poor lighting, occlusion, unusual camera angles, or deceptive behavior could weaken behavior, object, and context evidence.
